messages.subject: Zero inflated Poisson model
parts:
I have a zero-inflated Poisson model problem that I implemented in JAGS.  The data is about species response to environmental change.  This is a mixed model with density p(y) = pi+(1-pi)exp(-lambda), if y==0 and (1-pi)poisson(y, lambda) if y>0.  The JAGS model works fine for one species at a time.  When I pool all species together using a multilevel model, the JAGS model would not converge.  I was wondering whether Stan can do the trick.  I tried to use Stan this week and it worked for the single species model, but with very different results.

Here is the JAGS model:

  model{
    for (i in 1:n){
      y[i] ~ dpois(mu[i]);
      mu[i] <- (1-u[i])*lambda[i];
      u[i] ~ dbern(p0[i]);
      log(lambda[i]) <- beta[1]-beta[2]*x1[i]+beta[3]*log(x1[i]);
      logit(p0[i]) <- alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x2[i];
    }
    alpha[1] ~ dnorm(0,0.001);
    alpha[2] ~ dnorm(0,0.001)T(0,);

    logitEC50 <- -alpha[1]/alpha[2]
    beta[1] ~ dnorm(0, 0.001);
    beta[2] ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)T(0,);
    beta[3] ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)T(-1,);
  }

The priors on the regression coefficients are based on our understanding of the response pattern. For example, the slope of the logistic model is positive because we believe that the risk of a species disappearing increases as the environmental pressure increases. For the abundance model, ecological theory suggests that a species abundance along an environmental gradient is unimodal. I want to use a model similar to the gamma distribution density function, hence beta[2]>0 and beta[3]> -1.  The results fits the data very well.

Data <- dget("bosdata.Rdata")

bugs.in <- function(y=Data$y15, x=Data$NUII, n.chains=3){
  n <- length(y)
  iszero <- as.numeric(y==0)
  bugs.ini <- list()
  bugs.data <- list(NOBS=n, Y=y, x=x, iszero=iszero)
  for (i in 1:n.chains)
    bugs.ini [[i]] <- list(alpha=runif(2),
                           beta=runif(3))
  bugs.para <- c("alpha","beta")
  return(list(data=bugs.data, inits=bugs.ini, para=bugs.para,
              n.chains=n.chains,
              model="
                  data{
                    int<lower=0> NOBS;
                    real<lower=0> x[NOBS];
                    int<lower=0> Y[NOBS];
                    int iszero[NOBS];
                  }
                  parameters{
                    real alpha[2];
                    real beta[3];
                  }
                  model{
                    real lambda[NOBS];
                    real pi[NOBS];
       
                    alpha[1] ~ normal(10,100);
                    alpha[2] ~ normal(10,100)T[0,];

                    beta[1] ~ normal(0, 100);
                    beta[2] ~ normal(0, 100)T[0,];
                    beta[3] ~ normal(0, 100)T[-1,];

                    for(i in 1:NOBS) {
                      lambda[i] <- exp(beta[1]-beta[2]*x[i]+beta[3]*log(x[i]));
                      pi[i] <- inv_logit(alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x[i]);
                      lp__ <- lp__ + if_else(iszero[i], log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i])),
                                             log1m(pi[i])+poisson_log(Y[i], lambda[i]));
                    }
                  }
                  generated quantities{
                    real lambda[NOBS];
                    real pi[NOBS];
                    real logitEC50;

                    logitEC50 <- -alpha[1]/alpha[2];
                    for(i in 1:NOBS){
                      lambda[i] <- exp(beta[1]-beta[2]*x[i]+beta[3]*log(x[i]));
                      pi[i] <- inv_logit(alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x[i]);
                    }
                 }
                "))
  }

input.to.bugs <- bugs.in()
n.chains <- input.to.bugs$n.chains
n.iter <- 50000
n.keep <- 2000
thin <- max(c(1,floor((n.iter)*n.chains/n.keep)))

fit <- stan(model_code=input.to.bugs$model,
            data=input.to.bugs$data,init=input.to.bugs$inits,
            pars=input.to.bugs$para,
            iter=n.iter, thin=thin, chains=n.chains)
quartz()
plot(fit)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero inflated Poisson model
parts:
On 9/26/12 11:44 AM, Song wrote:
> I have a zero-inflated Poisson model problem that I implemented in JAGS.

> I tried to use
> Stan this week and it worked for the single species model, but with very different results.

Thanks for trying it out.

There are two issues. A bug on our end and an
error in coding your model. We're fixing the bug
for 1.0.2, but luckily in this case, recoding the model
with constraints will fix the problem in 1.0.1.

The model coding problem is that need to declare the parameters to
have constraints that match their truncations:

> ...

> parameters{
> real alpha[2];
> real beta[3];
> }
> model{

> alpha[1] ~ normal(10,100);
> alpha[2] ~ normal(10,100)T[0,];
>
> beta[1] ~ normal(0, 100);
> beta[2] ~ normal(0, 100)T[0,];
> beta[3] ~ normal(0, 100)T[-1,];

This means you need to define alpha[2], beta[2], and beta[3]
with constraints. This isn't directly possible in a Stan
array, which requires the same constraint on every entry.

So in this case, I'd just recode as

parameters
real alpha1;
real<lower=0> alpha2;
real beta1;
real<lower=0> beta2;
real<lower=-1> beta3;

>
> for(i in 1:NOBS) {
> lambda[i] <- exp(beta[1]-beta[2]*x[i]+beta[3]*log(x[i]));
> pi[i] <- inv_logit(alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x[i]);

It's a bit more efficient to define lambda and pi
to be scalars and reuse them (they don't need
to be arrays).

> lp__ <- lp__ + if_else(iszero[i], log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i])),
> log1m(pi[i])+poisson_log(Y[i], lambda[i]));

If lambda[i] gets too small (< -800 or so), the
exp(-lambda[i]) will overflow. In general, log_sum_exp
can be used to avoid the overflow:
log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i]))

==>

log_sum_exp(log(pi[i]),
log1m(pi[i]) - lambda[i]);

== log(exp(log(pi[i]))
+ exp(log(1 - pi[i])*exp(-lambda[i])))

Otherwise, everything looks OK on first glance.

> ...
> When using Stan, I wrote R script shown below. The estimated betas are close, but truncation is ignored.

Exactly! This is a bug in the current version of truncation
(which I'm about to fix). It doesn't check if the
values are outside the truncation range and reject.

I didn't think about that implementing it the first
time because the right way to implement it is with
the constraints. So if you put the constraints in,
it should pay attention to the constraints and do
the right thing.

> ...

> The estimated
> alphas are very different. I must have done something wrong

Your model should've worked as is, albeit slowly
and with the danger of getting stuck outside the
truncated support.

Version 1.0.2 should do the right thing with your
existing model, but it'll be relatively slow to sample.

The right way to code it for 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 is with
constraints.
> and would appreciate some help. Thank you very much.

Thanks again for letting us know and sending a detailed
error report. Please let us know if adding constraints
fixes the problem. It should.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero inflated Poisson model
parts:
This isn't a 1.0.1 vs. 1.0.2 issue if you have the
transforms matching your truncations. (I should've
also pointed out that if the truncation points are
constant, you don't even need the truncations -- the
probabilty is still right up to a proportion without it.)

Are you letting Stan do the initializations or
doing them yourself? If you are, the inits need to
be in the support or you'll get the error you report
because no step size will get the particle moving.

You can try running with the test_grad option to
see if the initialization is OK -- it'll print out
the unconstrained (transformed) initial values along with
the gradients computed by auto-dif and by finite diffs.
(The unconstrained params come in the same order as
the parameter declarations.)

The partials in the gradient should all be finite, or
there's a problem with the model specification at the
initialization point.

If you run this and still have problems that aren't
due to inits, could you send us a copy of the current model
and data, either to the list or to st...@mc-stan.org?

- Bob

be in the support or you'll get the error you report
because no step size will get the particle moving.

see if the initialization is OK -- it'll print out
the unconstrained (transformed) initial values along with
the gradients  computed by auto-dif and by finite diffs.

the parameter declarations.)

The partials in the gradient should all be finite, or
there's a problem with the model specification at the
initialization point.

    Thanks for trying it out.

    There are two issues.  A bug on our end and an
    error in coding your model.  We're fixing the bug
    for 1.0.2, but luckily in this case, recoding the model
    with constraints will fix the problem in 1.0.1.

    The model coding problem is that need to declare the parameters to
    have constraints that match their truncations:

     > ...

     >                    parameters{
     >                      real alpha[2];
     >                      real beta[3];
     >                    }
     >                    model{
    ...

     >                      alpha[1] ~ normal(10,100);
     >                      alpha[2] ~ normal(10,100)T[0,];
     >
     >                      beta[1] ~ normal(0, 100);
     >                      beta[2] ~ normal(0, 100)T[0,];
     >                      beta[3] ~ normal(0, 100)T[-1,];

    This means you need to define alpha[2], beta[2], and beta[3]
    with constraints.  This isn't directly possible in a Stan
    array, which requires the same constraint on every entry.

    So in this case, I'd just recode as

    parameters
       real alpha1;
       real<lower=0> alpha2;
       real beta1;
       real<lower=0> beta2;
       real<lower=-1> beta3;


     >
     >                      for(i in 1:NOBS) {
     >                        lambda[i] <- exp(beta[1]-beta[2]*x[i]+beta[__3]*log(x[i]));

     >                        pi[i] <- inv_logit(alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x[i]);

    It's a bit more efficient to define lambda and pi
    to be scalars and reuse them (they don't need
    to be arrays).


     >                        lp__ <- lp__ + if_else(iszero[i], log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i])),
     >                                               log1m(pi[i])+poisson_log(Y[i], lambda[i]));

    If lambda[i] gets too small (< -800 or so), the
    exp(-lambda[i]) will overflow.  In general, log_sum_exp
    can be used to avoid the overflow:


       log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i]))

       ==>

       log_sum_exp(log(pi[i]),
                   log1m(pi[i]) - lambda[i]);

        == log(exp(log(pi[i]))
               + exp(log(1 - pi[i])*exp(-lambda[i])))

    Otherwise, everything looks OK on first glance.

        ...


        When using Stan, I wrote R script shown below. The estimated betas are close, but truncation is ignored.


    Exactly!  This is a bug in the current version of truncation
    (which I'm about to fix).  It doesn't check if the
    values are outside the truncation range and reject.

    I didn't think about that implementing it the first
    time because the right way to implement it is with
    the constraints.  So if you put the constraints in,
    it should pay attention to the constraints and do
    the right thing.

     > ...

        The estimated
        alphas are very different.  I must have done something wrong

    and with the danger of getting stuck outside the
    truncated support.

    constraints.

    error report.    Please let us know if adding constraints
    fixes the problem.  It should.

    - Bob

messages.subject: how to submit model help requests
parts:
If you want help with models, please send
the following files as attachments with a
description of the problem you're having.

1. model file

2. data file

3. (optional) inits file

The data file can be created from R using
dump(list("var1",...)) or even better yet, using
stan_rdump() from the rstan package.

Make sure the data file has ALL the variables
listed in the data block of the model.

The reason I suggest this format of model and data
rather than an R program is that most of the developers,
including me, don't use Stan through RStan, and it's
also easier to instrument the code directly rather than
having to repackage and reinstall for R. Also, the
above format is easy to use through RStan, so it
works for everyone.

Thanks,

- Bob

On Wednesday, September 26, 2012 2:37:22 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
This isn't a 1.0.1 vs. 1.0.2 issue if you have the
transforms matching your truncations.  (I should've
also pointed out that if the truncation points are
constant, you don't even need the truncations -- the
probabilty is still right up to a proportion without it.)

Are you letting Stan do the initializations or
doing them yourself?  If you are, the inits need to
be in the support or you'll get the error you report
because no step size will get the particle moving.

You can try running with the test_grad option to
see if the initialization is OK -- it'll print out
the unconstrained (transformed) initial values along with
the gradients  computed by auto-dif and by finite diffs.
(The unconstrained params come in the same order as
the parameter declarations.)

The partials in the gradient should all be finite, or
there's a problem with the model specification at the
initialization point.

If you run this and still have problems that aren't
due to inits, could you send us a copy of the current model
and data, either to the list or to st...@mc-stan.org?

- Bob

On 9/26/12 2:05 PM, Song S. Qian wrote:
> Thank you very much for looking over my code. I made the changes you suggested that got the following error message:
>
> Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) :
>    No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?
>
> I will wait for 1.0.2.
>
> Song
>
> On Wed, Sep 26, 2012 at 1:34 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>     On 9/26/12 11:44 AM, Song wrote:
>      > I have a zero-inflated Poisson model problem that I implemented in JAGS.
>      > ...
>
>      > I tried to use
>      > Stan this week and it worked for the single species model, but with very different results.
>
>     Thanks for trying it out.
>
>     There are two issues.  A bug on our end and an
>     error in coding your model.  We're fixing the bug
>     for 1.0.2, but luckily in this case, recoding the model
>     with constraints will fix the problem in 1.0.1.
>
>     The model coding problem is that need to declare the parameters to
>     have constraints that match their truncations:
>
>      > ...
>
>      >                    parameters{
>      >                      real alpha[2];
>      >                      real beta[3];
>      >                    }
>      >                    model{
>     ...
>
>      >                      alpha[1] ~ normal(10,100);
>      >                      alpha[2] ~ normal(10,100)T[0,];
>      >
>      >                      beta[1] ~ normal(0, 100);
>      >                      beta[2] ~ normal(0, 100)T[0,];
>      >                      beta[3] ~ normal(0, 100)T[-1,];
>
>     This means you need to define alpha[2], beta[2], and beta[3]
>     with constraints.  This isn't directly possible in a Stan
>     array, which requires the same constraint on every entry.
>
>     So in this case, I'd just recode as
>
>     parameters
>        real alpha1;
>        real<lower=0> alpha2;
>        real beta1;
>        real<lower=0> beta2;
>        real<lower=-1> beta3;
>
>
>      >
>      >                      for(i in 1:NOBS) {
>      >                        lambda[i] <- exp(beta[1]-beta[2]*x[i]+beta[__3]*log(x[i]));
>      >                        pi[i] <- inv_logit(alpha[1] + alpha[2]*x[i]);
>
>     It's a bit more efficient to define lambda and pi
>     to be scalars and reuse them (they don't need
>     to be arrays).
>
>
>      >                        lp__ <- lp__ + if_else(iszero[i], log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i])),
>      >                                               log1m(pi[i])+poisson_log(Y[i], lambda[i]));
>
>     If lambda[i] gets too small (< -800 or so), the
>     exp(-lambda[i]) will overflow.  In general, log_sum_exp
>     can be used to avoid the overflow:
>
>
>        log(pi[i] + (1-pi[i]) * exp(-lambda[i]))
>
>        ==>
>
>        log_sum_exp(log(pi[i]),
>                    log1m(pi[i]) - lambda[i]);
>
>         == log(exp(log(pi[i]))
>                + exp(log(1 - pi[i])*exp(-lambda[i])))
>
>     Otherwise, everything looks OK on first glance.
>
>         ...
>
>
>         When using Stan, I wrote R script shown below. The estimated betas are close, but truncation is ignored.
>
>
>     Exactly!  This is a bug in the current version of truncation
>     (which I'm about to fix).  It doesn't check if the
>     values are outside the truncation range and reject.
>
>     I didn't think about that implementing it the first
>     time because the right way to implement it is with
>     the constraints.  So if you put the constraints in,
>     it should pay attention to the constraints and do
>     the right thing.
>
>      > ...
>
>         The estimated
>         alphas are very different.  I must have done something wrong
>
>
>     Your model should've worked as is, albeit slowly
>     and with the danger of getting stuck outside the
>     truncated support.
>
>     Version 1.0.2 should do the right thing with your
>     existing model, but it'll be relatively slow to sample.
>
>     The right way to code it for 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 is with
>     constraints.
>
>
>         and would appreciate some help.  Thank you very much.
>
>
>     Thanks again for letting us know and sending a detailed
>     error report.    Please let us know if adding constraints
>     fixes the problem.  It should.
>
>     - Bob
>
